reference.title: The kinds of date
reference.shortdesc: Seven ways to say how sure you are of a date, each with an example.

section.title: Say what the record says
section.p: A date in a family tree is often not exact. The kind of date lets the tree say so. Choose to see the kinds under . Pick the one that matches your evidence, not the one that sounds neatest.

row.entry: A copy of a parish register says that Emily Brontë was buried on 22 December 1848.
A record or a story gives a date that is close, but not exact.
A family story says that a great-uncle left home about 1850.
You worked the date out yourself, for example from an age.
A census says that a woman was 30 in 1851. You work out that she was born about 1821.
It happened on or before this date.
Branwell Brontë had drawing lessons before 1835.
It happened on or after this date.
Branwell worked as a portrait painter after his visit to London in 1835.
You know the earliest and the latest date it could have been.
A memorial tablet says that Maria Brontë died on 6 May 1825, in the 12th year of her age. So she was born between 7 May 1813 and 6 May 1814.
Something went on for a while, such as a job or a stay.
Patrick Brontë was curate of Thornton from 1815 to 1820.

section.title: A limit is not a guess
section.p: Use and for a limit that a record gives you. A baptism can be a limit on a birth, because a child is baptised after being born. Use only for a date that you worked out.

section.title: When two sources disagree
section.p: Do not pick one date and drop the other. Record each date with the source that gives it. Then your tree shows the disagreement, and a later record may settle it.
